After the Western Roman Empire fell, curved horns were common in Europe, while straight metal horns survived in the Middle East and Central Asia and came back to Europe after the Crusades. The folded tube appeared in the fifteenth century and the German semicircular horn in the eighteenth; Hanoverian light infantry used it in 1758, and it passed to Britain and became the bugle. Keyed bugles appeared in the nineteenth century, the Kent bugle was patented in Britain in 1811, and around 1850 they were mostly replaced by the cornet; after the middle of the nineteenth century bugles commonly gained valves.

Its playing is mostly limited to the few overtones of the bugle scale. It was also used for hunting signals and to announce coaches, and as a signal of peace when surrendering. Scout troops and boys' brigades use bugles too. In British and American military music the keyed bugle was widespread in the nineteenth century, and Richard Willis wrote for and played in the West Point band. At ceremonies and commemorations come bugle calls such as "The Last Post" and "Taps", played at funerals and on memorial days for the war dead.

The bugle is a brass instrument of simple construction, Hornbostel–Sachs 423.121.22, a lip-reed aerophone. It usually has no keys or means of adjusting pitch, and the tube is broadly conical; the player controls the pitch with lip vibration and breath and can sound only the few notes of the overtone series known as the bugle scale. It is used mainly for military calls — camp routine, cavalry orders and ceremonies — and also appears in scout troops and boys' brigades.

A beginner should first practise the few notes of the overtone series, the "bugle scale", and then extend the range. Because the pitch comes entirely from the player's breath and lip control, the basic order is: a steady breath, adjust the lip vibration, choose the target note from the overtone series.
